These petitions under Section 482 CrPC have been filed for quashing of proceedings of Case No.3478 of 2006, ''State Vs. Anil Behal and another' under Sections 272 and 273 IPC, arising out of Case Crime No.229 of 1999 lodged at Police Station Wazirganj, District Lucknow, pending in the Court of Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate (CBI), Lucknow.

sentences.text:
As it comes out, at the relevant time, the petitioner, Anil Shukla was working as Proprietor, M/s Shukla Sales and Service, which is C. & F. Agent of Pepsi Cola India, while petitioner, Anil Bahl was working as General Manager (Sales), M/s Pepsico India Holdings Private Limited, which Anil Shukla vs The State Of U.P. on 14 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/179095962/
1 manufactures and markets soft-drinks.

sentences.text: 3. As per the prosecution case, on 24.05.1999, the complainant purchased a bottle of cold-drink (Pepsi) from the Canteen situated at the premises of the High Court.
The complainant consumed some part of the cold-drink, and he found some insect/material inside the bottle.

Soon thereafter,
the complainant started omitting.
The complainant was rushed to the dispensary inside the High Court premises.
The Doctor, who attended the complainant, after examining, advised him to undergo some tests.

4. The complainant went to the police station with the bottle and lodged the aforesaid FIR against Pepsi Cola India Marketing Company C/o Shukla Sales and Service and Mr. Sanjay Jain, the owner of the Canteen fromwhere the complainant purchased the cold-drink.
It was also alleged that the Pepsi Bottle, which the complainant bought and consumed, was spurious and adulterated, and was not manufactured by the Company.
5. During the course of investigation, the police recorded statements of Rahul Dubey, Surya Kant Misra, Hans Chauhan and Arvind Kumar under Section 161 CrPC.
All these witnesses had stated that there was some creature or object at the bottom of the bottle.

The bottle, which was opened,
and some part of which was consumed on 24.05.1999, was analyzed by the Public Analyst on 04.08.2000, and the Public Analyst's report said that 'fungus' was found in it.
However, detail test could not be performed due to insufficient quantity of content in the bottle.
The bottle, which was bought and opened on 24.05.1999, was analyzed by Public Analyst after fifteen months of its opening.
6. The police, after investigation of the offence, had submitted the impugned charge-sheet under Section 272 and 273 IPC.
Though the petitioner, Anil Bahl was not named in the FIR, however, the charge-sheet had been filed against him also.
7. It is also case of the prosecution that on the next day of the incident i.e. on 25.05.1999 another bottle was purchased from the same canteen/shop and, it was also sent to the Public Analyst.

The Public Analyst, in his report, stated that so far sealed bottle was concerned, the sample was within the prescribed limit of the cold-drink, and no adulteration or any other deficiency was found in the contents of the sealed bottle.
8.

Beside, the statement of the complainant and some other witnesses recorded under Section 161 CrPC, as mentioned above, there was report of Public Analyst in respect of the bottle, which was purchased by the complainant on 24.05.1999, and on the basis of which the charge-sheet had been submitted for the offence under Sections 272 and 273 CrPC.
9.

Heard Mr. Rajesh Batra, learned Senior Advocate, assisted by Mr. Vikas Singh and Mr. Siddharth Sinha, learned counsels representing the petitioners, as well as Mr. Anurag Varma, learned Additional Government Advocate, and perused the files, including the Annexures attached therewith.

sentences.text: On behalf of the petitioners, it has been submitted that the Public Analyst, in its report, found fungus in the bottle, which was opened and consumed in part on 24.05.1999.
The report of the Public Analyst is dated 04.08.2000 i. e. fifteen months from the date of opening of the bottle and consumption of the same.
Even in respect of the sealed bottle, the expiry period is one year.
It should be consumed before the expiry period.
The Public Analyst had also said that because of insufficient quantity of contents of the opened bottle, detailed tests could not be conducted.
The learned counsel has, therefore, submitted that the report of the Public Analyst could not have been relied on by the police to file the charge-sheet under Section 272 and 273 IPC.

It has been further submitted that the offence under Sections 272 and 273 IPC were not attracted in the present case inasmuch as it was not an intentional adulteration, and sale of noxious cold-drink.
It has been further submitted that no complaint had been filed by the complainant under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as ''PFA Act').
The PFA Act is special statute which deals with offence of selling or distributing the adulterated food items, including cold-drinks.

The provisions of the IPC are general criminal provisions and, therefore, unless offence clearly attracts the general criminal provisions, the provisions of special statue for dealing with such an offence cannot be bypassed.

It has been further submitted that the offence, in the present case,
might come within the scope and ambit of PFA Act, but certainly the allegations do not constitute offence under Sections 272 and 273 IPC for which the charge-sheet had been filed, and after taking cognizance, the petitioners have been summoned.
11.

The learned counsels for the petitioners have placed reliance on the several judgments of the Supreme Court, including judgment in Pepsi Foods Limited and another Vs. Special Judicial Magistrate and others, (1998) 5 SCC 749.
12.

entities.text: Pepsi Foods Limited and another Vs. Special Judicial Magistrate and others, (1998) 5 SCC 749
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: On the other hand, on behalf of the State, it has been submitted by Mr. Anurag Varma, learned Additional Government Advocate, that the petitioners may appear before the trial Court, and file an application for discharge, if they are convinced that no offence is made out, and it is well within the power of trial Court to consider their application, and if it is found that no offence is made out, the trial Court is empowered to discharge them.

It has been, therefore, submitted that this Court should not exercise inherent power under Section 482 CrPC to quash the proceedings inasmuch as the entire record is before the trial Court, and the trial Court has ample power under the provisions of the CrPC to consider the material before framing of the charge(s), and if it is found that the offence is not made out, the trial Court can discharge the petitioners.
It is, therefore, submitted that this petition may be dismissed.
13. I have considered the submissions made by the learned counsels for the parties carefully.

14. Sections 272 and 273 IPC under which the charge-sheet has been filed and the petitioner has been summoned in Criminal Case No.2149 of 2014 read as under:-
"272. Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale.?Whoever adulterates any article of food or drink, so as to make such article noxious as food or drink, intending to sell such article as food or drink, or knowing it to be likely that the same will be sold as food or drink, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term Anil Shukla vs The State Of U.P. on 14 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/179095962/
3 which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.

entities.text: Anil Shukla vs The State Of U.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 273. Sale of noxious food or drink.?Whoever sells, or offers or exposes for sale, as food or drink, any article which has been rendered or has become noxious, or is in a state unfit for food or drink, knowing or having reason to believe that the same is noxious as food or drink, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both."
State Amendment .....

Uttar Pradesh- In Sections 272 and 273 for the words "shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both" the following shall be substituted, namely:- "shall be punished with imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine:
Provided that the court may, for adequate reasons to be mentioned in the judgment,
impose a sentence of imprisonment which is less than imprisonment for life.

15. To attract the offence under Section 272 IPC, following ingredients have to be present in the complaint:-
(i) adulteration in any article of food or drink;
(ii) because of adulteration, the food or drink articles has been rendered noxious;(iii)
intention to sell such adulterated article as food or drink; or (iv) there should be knowledge that such adulterated article of food or drink would be sold.
16.

Thus, adulteration of any article of food or drink has to be an intentional act on behalf of the accused and, further there should be intention of the accused to sell such an adulterated food item or he should know that the food item is adulterated and despite having knowledge, the accused has offered such adulterated item of food or drink for sale.
Unless and until these ingredients are clearly established in the complaint, the provisions of Section 272 IPC cannot be attracted.

17. Similarly, a person who himself might not have adulterated of any article of food or drink but if he has knowledge that the articles of food or drink offered by him for sale has been rendered or become noxious or it is not fit for consumption then only Section 273 IPC is attracted.
To attract Section 273 IPC there has to be knowledge of the accused offering article of food or drink for sale that such a article has been rendered noxious or unfit for consumption.

sentences.text: The allegations in the FIR have been noted above.

There is no allegation that the petitioner knowingly that food article in question has been rendered noxious has offered it for sale or the petitioner intentionally adulterated the food article and offered it for sale.

The presumption of intention or knowledge cannot be drawn to attract the provisions of Sections 272 and 273 IPC.
19.

The Supreme Court in the case of Director of Enforcement versus M.C.T.M. Corporation Pvt.
Ltd. and others: (1996) 2 SCC 471 in para 7 while defining mens rea has held as under:-
"7.

entities.text:
Director of Enforcement versus M.C.T.M. Corporation Pvt.
Ltd. and others: (1996) 2 SCC 471
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "Mens rea" is a state of mind.

Under the criminal law, mens rea is considered as the "guilty intention" and unless it is found that the "accused" had the guilty intention to commit the "crime" he cannot be held "guilty" of committing the crime.
An "offence" under Criminal Procedure Code and the General Clauses Act, 1897 is defined as any act or omission "made punishable by any law for the time being in force".
The proceedings under Section 23(1)(a) of FERA, 1947 are "adjudicatory" in nature and character and are not "criminal proceedings".
The officers of the Enforcement Directorate and other administrative authorities are expressly empowered by the Act to "adjudicate" only.

Indeed they have to act "judicially" and follow the rules of natural justice to the extent applicable but, they are not "Judges"
of the "Criminal Courts" trying an "accused" for commission of an offence, as understood in the general context.
They perform quasi-judicial functions and do not act as "courts" but only as "administrators" and "adjudicators".

In the proceedings before them, they do not try "an accused" for commission of "any crime" (not merely an offence) but determine the liability of the contravenor for the breach of his "obligations" imposed under the Act.
They impose "penalty" for the breach of the "civil obligations" laid down under the Act and not impose any "sentence" for the commission of an offence.
The expression "penalty" is a word of wide significance.
Sometimes, it means recovery of an amount as a penal measure even in civil proceedings.
An exaction which is not compensatory in character is also termed as a "penalty".

When penalty is imposed by an adjudicating officer, it is done so in "adjudicatory proceedings" and not by way of fine as a result of "prosecution" of an "accused" for commission of an "offence" in a criminal court.
Therefore, merely because "penalty" clause exists in Section 23(1)(a), the nature of the proceedings under that section is not changed from "adjudicatory" to "criminal" prosecution.

An order made by an adjudicating authority under the Act is not that of conviction but of determination of the breach of the civil obligation by the offender."
20.

The Supreme Court in State of Haryana and others vs. Ch. Bhajan Lal and others reported in AIR 1992 SC 604, has summarised the conditions, under which the Court may consider quashing of proceedings, in the following terms:-
"108.

sentences.text:
In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code which we have extracted Anil Shukla vs The State Of U.P. on 14 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/179095962/
5 and reproduced above, we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such powers should be exercised.
1.

entities.text: Anil Shukla vs The State Of U.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Where the allegations made in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.

2. Where the allegations in the First Information Report and other materials, if any,
accompanying the F.I.R. do not disclose a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code.

3. Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.

4. Where, the allegations in the F.I.R. do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation is permitted by a police officer without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code.
5.

Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
6.

Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party.

7. Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with malafide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge."

sentences.text: The issue being examined in the instant case is the jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., if it chooses to quash the initiation of the prosecution against an accused, at the stage of issuing process, or at the stage of committal, or even at the stage of framing of charges.
These are all stages before the commencement of the actual trial.
The same parameters would naturally be available for later stages as well.

The power vested in the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C., at the stages referred to hereinabove, would have far reaching consequences,
inasmuch as, it would negate the prosecution's/complainant's case without allowing the prosecution/complainant to lead evidence.
Such a determination must always be rendered with caution, care and circumspection.

To invoke its inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. the High Court has to be fully satisfied, that the material produced by the accused is such, that would lead to the conclusion, that his/their defence is based on sound, reasonable, and indubitable facts; the material produced is such, as would rule out and displace the assertions contained in the charges levelled against the accused; and the material produced is such, as would clearly reject and overrule the veracity of the allegations contained in the accusations levelled by the prosecution/complainant.
It should be sufficient to rule out, reject and discard the accusations levelled by the prosecution/complainant, without the necessity of recording any evidence.
For this the material relied upon by the defence should not have been refuted, or alternatively, cannot be justifiably refuted, being material of sterling and impeccable quality.
The material relied upon by the accused should be such, as would persuade a reasonable person to dismiss and condemn the actual basis of the accusations as false.

In such a situation, the judicial conscience of the High Court would persuade it to exercise its power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash such criminal proceedings, for that would prevent abuse of process of the court, and secure the ends of justice.

30. Based on the factors canvassed in the foregoing paragraphs, we would delineate the following steps to determine the veracity of a prayer for quashing, raised by an accused by invoking the power vested in the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C.:
30.1.

Step one, whether the material relied upon by the accused is sound, reasonable,
and indubitable, i.e., the material is of sterling and impeccable quality?

30.2. Step two, whether the material relied upon by the accused, would rule out the assertions contained in the charges levelled against the accused, i.e., the material is sufficient to reject and overrule the factual assertions contained in the complaint, i.e.,
the material is such, as would persuade a reasonable person to dismiss and condemn the factual basis of the accusations as false?

30.3. Step three, whether the material relied upon by the accused, has not been refuted by the prosecution/complainant; and/or the material is such, that it cannot be justifiably refuted by the prosecution/complainant?
Anil Shukla vs The State Of U.P. on 14 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/179095962/
7 30.4.

entities.text: Anil Shukla vs The State Of U.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Step four, whether proceeding with the trial would result in an abuse of process of the court, and would not serve the ends of justice"
(Emphasized by me) 30.5.

If the answer to all the steps is in the affirmative, judicial conscience of the High Court should persuade it to quash such criminal proceedings, in exercise of power vested in it under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C.

Such exercise of power, besides doing justice to the accused,
would save precious court time, which would otherwise be wasted in holding such a trial (as well as,
proceedings arising therefrom) specially when, it is clear that the same would not conclude in the conviction of the accused."
22.

The Supreme Court in the case of State of Maharashtra and others Vs. Sayyed Hassan Sayyed Subhan & Ors: 2018 SCC OnLine SC 1580 has held a prosecution under IPC unless expressly or impliedly barred, offence can be tried under the IPC as well as under specific enactments.

entities.text: State of Maharashtra and others Vs. Sayyed Hassan Sayyed Subhan & Ors: 2018 SCC OnLine SC 1580
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There is no bar to a trial or conviction of an offender under two different enactments, but the bar is only to the punishment of the offender twice for the offence.

23. Supreme Court in the aforesaid judgment has set aside the judgment of the High Court that the action against the factories who were transporting and selling Gutka/Pan Masala cannot be taken under the IPC and can be initiated only under the provisions of Food and Safety Standards Act,
2006 (hereinafter referred to as 'FSS Act').

Therefore, the submission of the learned Senior Advocate that since act constitutes an offence under the provisions of FSS Act, filing of charge-sheet under Sections 272 and 273 IPC was not proper, has no force and is rejected.

However, considering the allegations in FIR and absence of intention or knowledge regarding adulteration and selling of the food items, I am of the view that the provisions of Sections 272 and 273 IPC are not attracted.
24. Considering the facts of the present case and the provisions of Sections 272 and 273 IPC, it would meet the interest of justice if the impugned proceedings are quashed.
25. Thus, both the petitions are allowed.

Consequently, all proceedings, arising out of Case Crime No.229 of 1999 lodged at Police Station Wazirganj, District Lucknow, including Case No.3478 of 2006, ''State Vs. Anil Behal and another' under Sections 272 and 273 IPC, pending in the Court of Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate (CBI), Lucknow are quashed.
